questions.question: Describe the path of light through the eye from the cornea to the retina, naming the function of each structure it passes through.
questions.expected_answer: Light enters through the cornea, the transparent curved front, which refracts it and does most of the focusing. It passes through the aqueous humour and the pupil, the opening in the iris; the iris controls the pupil size and so the amount of light entering (small in bright light, large in dim light). The lens refracts the light further and fine-tunes the focus by changing shape (accommodation, controlled by the ciliary muscle). Light passes through the vitreous humour and forms an inverted image on the retina, which contains light-sensitive rods and cones.

questions.question: Explain how the lens changes to focus on a near object and a distant object. Why is the image on the retina inverted, and how is it that we see the world the right way up?
questions.expected_answer: For a distant object the ciliary muscle relaxes, the ligaments tighten and the lens is pulled thin and flat, bending light less. For a near object the ciliary muscle contracts, the ligaments slacken and the elastic lens becomes fatter and more curved, bending light more. This is accommodation. Rays from the top of the object cross over as they pass through the cornea and lens and land at the bottom of the retina (and vice versa), so the image is inverted, as in a pinhole camera. The brain interprets the nerve signals so that we perceive the world upright.

questions.question: Compare rods and cones. Explain how light is turned into a signal the brain can use, and explain why you see only shades of grey in a dark room.
questions.expected_answer: Rods: about 120 million, very sensitive to dim light, no colour (black, white, grey), spread mainly around the edges of the retina, used for night vision and movement. Cones: about 6 million, need brighter light, detect colour and fine detail, three types (roughly red, green, blue), concentrated in the fovea. Light changes the shape of a pigment molecule in a receptor cell, triggering chemical changes that produce a nerve impulse; impulses travel along the optic nerve to the visual area of the brain, which interprets them as an image. In a dark room only rods are stimulated, and rods do not distinguish colours, so we see in grey.
